column4: The section calls a guide هادٍ because he goes ahead of the traveler; this ayah asks whether the one who يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ is more worthy to be followed than one who needs guidance, making the guide/follower relation explicit.

In Moses's answer to Pharaoh, this ayah says God made the earth a resting place, laid سُبُلًا through it, and sent down rain; the section's traveler gains an earthly route and provision in the same Moses discourse.

The section's traveler moves from a hidden way at night to a visible route; this ayah compares one given نُورًا يَمْشِي بِهِ among people with someone in darkness unable to emerge, a direct walking-and-light parallel.
The section ties guidance to a path made visible; this ayah promises believers a light by which they walk, نُورًا تَمْشُونَ بِهِ, making illumination usable as a guide.

The section says the Prophet lacked knowledge of the Book and faith before being made a guide; this ayah says a Messenger teaches the Book and wisdom to a people formerly in ضَلَالٍ مُبِينٍ, joining teaching with release from error.

The section ties the Prophet's former lack of knowledge to his later guidance; this ayah describes God's favor in sending a Messenger who recites and teaches the Book and wisdom to people who had been in ضَلَالٍ مُبِينٍ.

The section says the Prophet did not know the Book and faith before God guided him; this ayah says God taught him وَعَلَّمَكَ مَا لَمْ تَكُن تَعْلَمُ and gave him the Book and wisdom, naming that gift as God's favor.

The section's root ض ل ل covers leaving the intended way; this ayah has a speaker say that a companion led him astray from the Reminder after it came, a specific account of a companion diverting someone from guidance.
The section says a road appears at ضُحَى; this oath names the day when it جَلَّاهَا, making day the time when what was hidden is brought to view.

The section makes a route visible after darkness; this ayah says نُورٌ وَكِتَابٌ مُّبِينٌ have come, and 5:16 continues by describing guidance to paths of peace, so this row supplies the light that its neighbor turns into a way.
The section recalls Moses finding guidance while traveling; this ayah describes Moses being sent to bring his people مِنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ, a direct Moses-and-wayfinding parallel.
The section defines هداية as gentle direction; this command tells the Prophet to invite to سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ with wisdom and good counsel, making the manner of guidance concrete.

The section defines guidance as direction with gentleness and develops Moses's journeys; here God tells Moses and Aaron to speak to Pharaoh with قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا, a specific way of addressing someone toward remembrance.

The section contrasts the unseen night road with visible daylight; this ayah describes God taking believers يُخْرِجُهُم مِّنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ, while the opposite movement is assigned to disbelief.
The section's night traveler cannot see the road; this oath names the night as it يَغْشَى, covering what is there.
The section says the road appears when daylight comes; this oath names the day as it تَجَلَّى, the counterpart to the night that covers in 92:1.
The section describes a traveler searching for a mosque or home; this ayah sends pilgrims مِن كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ, on foot and by camel, while 22:26 supplies the House as their destination.
The section links remembrance and speaking of God's favor with having been guided; the people of the Garden say هَدَانَا لِهَذَا, naming their arrival as the result of guidance.
The section's guide goes ahead for a traveler to follow; this ayah portrays someone regretting that he did not take سَبِيلًا مَعَ الرَّسُولِ, a concrete failure to follow the guide.
The section makes guidance bodily visible as a road emerging into daylight; this ayah develops a lamp-and-light image and says يَهْدِي اللَّهُ لِنُورِهِ, a specific illumination-as-guidance parallel.

The section calls a guide هادٍ because he precedes the traveler; on the Day of Judgment this ayah puts believers' light, نُورُهُم بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ, before them as they are given news of the Garden, a specific light-leading-to-destination image.
The section pairs travel with hope that God will guide the traveler; Abraham says he is going to his Lord and that He will guide him, سَيَهْدِينِ.

The section says the Prophet was taught what he had not known and then became a guide; this ayah describes the Messenger teaching the Book and wisdom and وَيُعَلِّمُكُم مَّا لَمْ تَكُونُوا تَعْلَمُونَ.

The section's root note says a road دَحَا when it appeared; this ayah uses دَحَاهَا for spreading the earth after 79:29 describes night darkening and daylight emerging. The sense differs, so this is only a tentative reminder of the ground on which a revealed route lies.

The section gives a secondary dictionary sense of هادية as a staff that goes before its holder; this ayah asks Moses what is in his right hand, and 20:18 identifies it as his staff and says he leans on it. The staff matches the object, though this passage does not use it to find a route.
The section's guide precedes the traveler toward a destination; Pharaoh instead يَقْدُمُ قَوْمَهُ toward the Fire, a direct reversal in which leading the way ends at ruin.
The section presents the guide as one who leads toward a way; this ayah says Pharaoh's people were made أَئِمَّةً يَدْعُونَ إِلَى النَّارِ, leaders whose direction is the opposite of guidance.
